title: Benchmark methodology review (workloads, prompt sets, variance + disclaimers)
summary: Working session to lock v1 benchmark methodology for the public latency/$ report. The group aligned on: (1) workload definitions (prefill/decode mixes, context/output sizes, concurrency points), (2) prompt set selection (v3 “production mix” with documented distributions and exclusions), and (3) how we’ll present variance and disclaimers to avoid overclaiming. Open items remain on exact rerun thresholds for stability gates and whether streaming latency is included in v1 charts or kept as a secondary metric/tool-tip.
topics: Workload grid: context length + output length buckets, prefill-heavy vs decode-heavy mixes
Caching + batching policy: what’s on by default vs what’s “tuned”
Warmup and run duration; repeats and stability gates
Prompt set v3 composition + exclusions (safety-filtered prompts, very long-tail contexts)
Variance presentation: p50/p95, confidence bands, rerun-on-variance thresholds
Metric naming: latency/$ vs cost efficiency; supporting metrics ($/1M tokens, tok/s)
Disclaimers + claims safety: “results vary by workload/region/config” and reproducibility artifacts
next_steps: Claire to post the final workload grid (tables + definitions) to Confluence and tag Jonas/Nadia for sign-off.
Rina to finalize prompt set v3 manifest and document sampling rules + exclusions.
Nadia to confirm the normalization rules for latency/$ and draft a plain-English explanation for the report methodology section.
Elliot + Wei to draft the public-facing variance + disclaimer language for the landing page and PDF methodology summary.
Soojin to schedule a 30-min legal pre-read (Michael Grant / Sofia Mendes) once the above text is drafted.
action_items: Claire Dubois — Share v1 workload grid (context/output buckets, prefill/decode mixes, concurrency points) in Confluence with definitions — Due 2025-06-12
Rina Kobayashi — Lock prompt set v3 manifest + document sampling/exclusions; add linkable run IDs — Due 2025-06-13
Nadia Rahman — Write 1-paragraph “what is latency/$” explainer + confirm formula inputs (p95 vs blended) — Due 2025-06-12
Elliot Price — Draft disclaimers + variance language for PDF + web tooltips; include ‘results vary’ + ‘not a guarantee’ — Due 2025-06-14
Wei Chen — Propose landing page methodology summary structure (bullets + link to full methodology) — Due 2025-06-14
Soojin Lee — Book legal claims review pre-read once drafts ready; align on do-not-say list — Due 2025-06-17
transcript_text:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Benchmark methodology review (workloads, prompt sets, variance + disclaimers)
Date: 2025-06-10
Start time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 58 min
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees:
- Soojin Lee (PMM, Redwood)
- Ethan Wallace (Content Marketing, Redwood)
- Jonas Weber (Dir Performance & Evals, Redwood)
- Claire Dubois (Sr Research Engineer, Redwood)
- Rina Kobayashi (Perf Benchmarks, Redwood)
- Nadia Rahman (Cost attribution / latency/$ metric, Redwood)
- Elliot Price (Docs, Redwood)
- Wei Chen (Docs/Tech copy, Redwood)
- Talia Benson (Program Mgmt, Redwood)


00:00 Soojin Lee: Alright, thanks everyone. This is the methodology review, specifically workload definitions, prompt sets, and then how we talk about variance and disclaimers publicly. Goal is “no surprises” when we go to Legal and when we ship the landing page.

00:18 Ethan Wallace: Yeah and selfishly I need like… the words. Like the sentences we can say without getting yelled at on Twitter.

00:24 Jonas Weber: (laughs) Please don’t write “fastest on earth” or whatever.

00:28 Soojin Lee: Exactly. Okay, Claire, can you start with where we are on workload grid? I saw the working doc but I want to make sure we’re aligned on the final buckets.

00:40 Claire Dubois: Sure. So, currently we have three primary workload “shapes”. We’re trying to capture prefill heavy, decode heavy, and balanced. The context/output buckets are roughly: 1k in / 256 out, 4k in / 512 out, and 8k in / 1k out. Not exact, but those are the targets.

01:03 Rina Kobayashi: And we sample prompts to hit those lengths, like we pad by selecting prompts, we’re not literally padding tokens.

01:10 Claire Dubois: Right, right. We’re selecting prompts whose tokenization lands in those bands. Then concurrency points—this is the part I want to debate—are 1, 8, 32. We had 64 in earlier drafts but it got too noisy and queueing dominated.

01:29 Jonas Weber: Also 64 is not realistic for a lot of customers unless they’re doing heavy batching, and then we’re benchmarking “who batches best” more than raw serving.

01:39 Nadia Rahman: Just to flag, on the metric side, concurrency impacts both cost and latency. If we publish a single number, people will ask “what concurrency is that?”. So we need to decide if we blend concurrency or pick a representative point.

01:53 Soojin Lee: Yeah. For the public report we want to avoid like a matrix explosion, but we can’t hide the setup.

02:01 Ethan Wallace: Could we do a default concurrency, like 8, and then show 1 and 32 as a sensitivity chart? Like “here’s how it changes.”

02:10 Claire Dubois: That’s basically what I’d recommend. If you pick concurrency 1, you’re benchmarking kernel selection and network. If you pick 32, you’re benchmarking queueing and batching policies and maybe we get accused of tuning.

02:24 Rina Kobayashi: Also 32 is where the p95 gets weird if there’s any background fleet variance.

02:30 Jonas Weber: There’s also region capacity. When the region is slightly constrained, the tail explodes at higher concurrency and people will think we’re lying.

02:39 Soojin Lee: Okay, so directionally: primary comparisons at concurrency 8, and we publish 1 and 32 as “additional views”. Is that a lock?

02:48 Claire Dubois: I’m comfortable with that.

02:50 Nadia Rahman: Yes, but we need to say it. Like in methodology: “primary metric uses concurrency=8.”

02:56 Wei Chen: From a docs standpoint we can do a callout box “What we measured” and list it as bullets.

03:03 Soojin Lee: Great. Now prompt sets. Rina, can you talk v3? I saw PR-4840 reference.

03:10 Rina Kobayashi: Yeah, PR-4840 adds prompt set v3, we’re calling it “production mix”. It’s meant to reflect distributions we see: some short chat turns, some longer RAG-ish contexts, and some summarization. We removed a few that were like extremely long tail—like 40k context stuff—because it made the run time too big and also not supported across all models.

03:36 Ethan Wallace: Wait, we’re excluding 40k because of runtime, or because it’s not apples-to-apples?

03:42 Rina Kobayashi: Both. Some models we’re listing don’t support that context, or they do but with different rope scaling, and then it becomes “which rope trick” rather than serving.

03:53 Jonas Weber: We can still mention long-context as “future work” but not in v1.

03:59 Claire Dubois: The other exclusion is anything that would trigger safety blocks inconsistently across vendors. Like if we were to compare competitor APIs, we don’t want a prompt that gets refused by one and answered by another, because then you’re not measuring latency, you’re measuring policy.

04:16 Soojin Lee: That’s an important disclaimer. “We exclude prompts likely to be refused.”

04:21 Wei Chen: Noted.

04:23 Nadia Rahman: Also we should be explicit: we’re not scoring output quality here. So we need to keep prompts stable and not optimize prompts for one model.

04:31 Ethan Wallace: I can already hear the critique: “They cherry picked prompts that their stack likes.”

04:36 Jonas Weber: So we publish the prompt set manifest, or at least the categories and token distributions, and the sampling rules. We can’t publish raw prompts if there’s licensing or PII risk, but we can publish hashes and lengths.

04:51 Elliot Price: That’s consistent with what we’ve done before. Public artifact with: prompt_id hash, in_tokens, out_tokens target, category label.

04:59 Soojin Lee: Okay. Let’s move to caching/batching policy because this is where it gets contentious. Claire, what’s “default” for Redwood for this benchmark? What’s on? What’s off?

05:10 Claire Dubois: So, Redwood runtime by default uses continuous batching. That’s not optional unless you disable it. For caching: prefix caching is on, but only when the prompt repeats. Our prompt set is mostly unique prompts, so caching doesn’t materially help, unless the harness repeats the same prompt for warmup.

05:29 Rina Kobayashi: We do warmup runs, yes. But we exclude them from measurement.

05:33 Claire Dubois: Exactly. KV cache is obviously part of decode, that’s just “how transformers work,” not the caching feature. People confuse that.

05:41 Nadia Rahman: For the report, we should avoid the word “caching” without specifying “prefix caching across requests” versus “KV cache within a request.”

05:50 Ethan Wallace: Great point. I don’t want to get dunked on because we used a normal KV cache.

05:55 Jonas Weber: Every vendor uses KV cache. The question is cross-request reuse, and we’re not depending on that for the headline.

06:04 Soojin Lee: So disclaimers should say: “We did not rely on cross-request prefix cache; prompts are predominantly unique; standard model KV caching is used as normal inference.”

06:15 Elliot Price: I can wordsmith that.

06:17 Wei Chen: Same. We can put it in the FAQ too.

06:20 Soojin Lee: Cool. Now variance and stability. Jonas, can you walk through what we’ll publish? p50/p95, repeats, error bars, etc.

06:31 Jonas Weber: Sure. Minimum: publish p50 and p95 latency and throughput. For “latency/$” we’re currently computing it as cost per token times latency—well, sorry—let me say it correctly: it’s “milliseconds per dollar” or “latency per dollar spent” normalized. Nadia can correct me.

06:49 Nadia Rahman: (interrupts) Yeah, the way we implemented in PR-4821 is basically: latency/$ = p50 latency divided by dollars per request, and dollars per request is derived from $/1M tokens times tokens per request, adjusted for prefill/decode tokens. But we might decide to use p95 latency in numerator for public metric.

07:08 Ethan Wallace: Which is safer? p50 makes us look good, but p95 is what customers care about.

07:13 Claire Dubois: p95 is noisier though.

07:15 Rina Kobayashi: Way noisier across regions.

07:18 Jonas Weber: My recommendation: headline uses a blended measure: p50 for “typical”, but we always show p95 alongside and we do not hide it. And we add a stability note: “results are median of N runs” and “p95 variance threshold.”

07:33 Soojin Lee: What’s N? Three? Five?

07:36 Rina Kobayashi: For region sweeps we can do 5 repeats, but that’s expensive.

07:41 Claire Dubois: If we do 3, a flake can contaminate. If we do 5, it’s more robust.

07:46 Nadia Rahman: For cost metric, we also need enough samples so the cost estimate isn’t dominated by one run’s utilization anomaly.

07:54 Jonas Weber: I’d say 5 for primary regions, maybe 3 for long-tail, but for a public report I’d rather be consistent.

08:03 Soojin Lee: Consistency matters for messaging.

08:05 Ethan Wallace: Also if we say “five runs”, people trust it more.

08:09 Claire Dubois: Then we need to schedule the capacity reservations accordingly.

08:12 Talia Benson: I can note that as a dependency for Vanessa’s capacity plan.

08:15 Jonas Weber: On variance: We can include either error bars or a shaded band. But on a marketing page, error bars confuse people.

08:24 Wei Chen: Tooltips. Like “Why do these numbers move?” We can say “typical variance across runs: X%.”

08:31 Elliot Price: Also we can do a methodology section with a plain-language explanation: fleet variance, background noise, network.

08:38 Ethan Wallace: What about the “rerun if variance above threshold” gating? That was in the stability PR, 4855.

08:45 Rina Kobayashi: PR-4855 adds: if p95 latency variance exceeds a threshold—currently 7% across repeats—we auto-rerun. But we need to decide: is it 7, 10, and is it per region or global.

08:59 Claire Dubois: 7% is aggressive. It triggers reruns often in APAC.

09:04 Jonas Weber: But if we publish APAC with huge variance, we’ll get called out. I’d keep 7% but set a maximum reruns cap.

09:12 Nadia Rahman: Or we present APAC as “preview region” with a disclaimer. But I think Sales will hate that.

09:18 Soojin Lee: Let’s not introduce “preview” unless we have to. Another option: publish the median and add “range across runs” as a tooltip.

09:27 Wei Chen: That’s doable. E.g., “p95 range: 410–460ms.”

09:32 Ethan Wallace: Okay but please don’t make the chart look like a science paper.

09:36 Jonas Weber: This is a benchmark report. It should look like a little science paper.

09:40 (crosstalk)

09:42 Soojin Lee: (laughs) We can make it readable. Alright, next: how to describe regions and capacity. Claire mentioned earlier queueing. What are we saying publicly?

09:54 Claire Dubois: We should say: runs were performed in specific named cloud regions, on specific hardware types, during a defined window, and with reserved capacity to reduce noise. Still, shared components like networking can introduce variance.

10:09 Nadia Rahman: And we should avoid “guarantee” language. Like, “your mileage may vary.”

10:13 Elliot Price: “Performance depends on request shape, concurrency, and region; published numbers are not an SLA.” That kind of thing.

10:20 Soojin Lee: Yes. Also: “benchmarks reflect Redwood configuration at the time; we’ll publish run manifests.”

10:27 Rina Kobayashi: For reproducibility: we can publish a Docker runner image reference, but maybe not full internal scripts.

10:35 Jonas Weber: The runner is in PR-4888, dockerized. We can share a public-friendly version or at least say “we use pinned dependencies and manifests.”

10:44 Ethan Wallace: Question: Are we comparing to competitors in this v1 methodology write-up? Or do we keep it Redwood-only?

10:52 Soojin Lee: Marketing wants context but Legal will be conservative. For today, just ensure the methodology can support competitor baselines “where appropriate, with caveats.”

11:01 Jonas Weber: If we include competitor APIs, we have to be explicit about their default settings, rate limits, and how we measured. Some don’t expose the same knobs.

11:11 Claire Dubois: And the biggest trap: some providers use aggressive caching behind the scenes or different streaming behaviors. If we measure end-to-end, it’s not strictly comparable.

11:22 Nadia Rahman: Also, cost normalization. Their pricing might be list price vs committed use. We must specify “public list pricing at time of test.”

11:32 Wei Chen: That goes into a footnote.

11:34 Elliot Price: And in the “claims” doc we’ll need a do-not-say list. Like we can’t say “X is 2x cheaper” without qualifying.

11:43 Soojin Lee: Right. That’s in the enablement message house, but for now we’ll bake safe language.


12:00 Soojin Lee: Let’s go deeper on how we define “latency/$” in words. Nadia, can you give me the one sentence.

12:06 Nadia Rahman: One sentence… okay: “Latency per dollar measures the time-to-first-token or end-to-end latency you get for each dollar spent generating a response, based on measured latency and published per-token pricing under a fixed workload.”

12:23 Ethan Wallace: That’s a little dense.

12:25 Nadia Rahman: Yeah. Alternative: “It’s a cost-efficiency metric that combines speed and price—how fast you can generate a typical response for a given spend.”

12:36 Wei Chen: We can do both: a short sentence and then a more precise definition in the methodology accordion.

12:43 Jonas Weber: Also specify what latency we use—E2E vs model-only.

12:47 Claire Dubois: We should use end-to-end (request to last token) because customers care. But we should also log model-only for debugging.

12:55 Rina Kobayashi: The harness captures both. But we need to make sure we’re consistent with streaming.

13:00 Soojin Lee: Streaming is the next topic. Are we including streaming metrics in v1?

13:06 Jonas Weber: I vote: yes, but not in the headline. We include TTFT (time to first token) and steady-state tokens/sec in the appendix or interactive view.

13:16 Ethan Wallace: That’s basically what the community will ask: “TTFT matters for chat.”

13:21 Claire Dubois: But TTFT is super sensitive to network and queueing. If we show it without context, it becomes “Redwood is slower in EU” even if it’s a transient.

13:31 Nadia Rahman: And TTFT doesn’t map cleanly to the cost metric. You can have low TTFT but then slow decode.

13:38 Wei Chen: Maybe: We default to end-to-end in the table, and we offer toggles for TTFT and tok/s with disclaimers.

13:45 Soojin Lee: That matches the PRD direction, I think.

13:48 Elliot Price: For disclaimers: “TTFT is measured client-side; may vary with network.”

13:55 Jonas Weber: Exactly.


14:02 Ethan Wallace: Can I ask about warmup? Because people will say “you excluded cold start.”

14:07 Rina Kobayashi: We do warmup requests to stabilize kernels and caches. We’re measuring steady-state performance, not cold start. That’s intentional.

14:15 Claire Dubois: And cold start is mostly a capacity management story, not runtime. If we include cold start we’re measuring how often a pod was evicted.

14:25 Jonas Weber: But we should say it: “warmup excluded; steady-state.”

14:28 Soojin Lee: Okay. So disclaimers include: steady-state, warm caches for the service, but not relying on cross-request prefix caching.

14:36 Nadia Rahman: Not “warm caches” as in prefix cache. Just “service warmed.” Wording matters.

14:41 Soojin Lee: Great catch.


14:45 Talia Benson: Quick check: Are we deciding on the exact run window? Like “June 17–June 24” etc.

14:51 Jonas Weber: We’ll have the window in the report, yes. Once region sweeps complete.

14:56 Soojin Lee: Okay.


15:00 (discussion continues; minor edits and clarifications)

15:06 Wei Chen: On the landing page, I propose a “Methodology at a glance” block:
- Regions tested
- Hardware class
- Concurrency=8 for headline
- Prompt set v3 categories
- Runs repeated N times; median reported
- Metrics: p50/p95, latency/$, $/1M tokens
And then “Read full methodology” link.

15:25 Ethan Wallace: Love it.

15:26 Claire Dubois: As long as it includes the detail that prompt set is sampled to token length buckets.

15:31 Wei Chen: Yes.


15:33 Elliot Price: For variance language, propose something like: “We repeat each measurement five times and report the median. If tail latency variance exceeds a threshold, we rerun. You may see small differences due to region/network variability.”

15:49 Jonas Weber: That’s accurate.

15:51 Soojin Lee: What’s the threshold number we want to put publicly? Do we say 7%?

15:57 Rina Kobayashi: If we publish 7% and later change it, people will say we moved goalposts.

16:02 Claire Dubois: We could say “predefined threshold” without giving the exact number.

16:07 Ethan Wallace: Won’t that look shady?

16:10 Jonas Weber: I think it’s okay to be specific. Being specific builds trust. If we change it, we publish a changelog.

16:18 Soojin Lee: Okay, we can be specific but we need to be ready to own it.

16:22 Nadia Rahman: And the threshold might differ for p95 vs p50. But we can state it’s on p95.

16:28 Soojin Lee: Great.


16:32 Ethan Wallace: One more thing: People will ask if we tuned per model. Like quantization, kernel, whatever.

16:38 Claire Dubois: We use Redwood-verified profiles. That is “normal operation.” But we’re not hand-tuning per benchmark run. We pin model versions and config.

16:48 Rina Kobayashi: The manifest includes model version, quantization profile if any, and runtime flags.

16:54 Jonas Weber: So disclaimer: “Models run with standard Redwood serving profiles; no per-run manual tuning.”

17:01 Elliot Price: Might want to say “no benchmark-specific tuning.”

17:05 Soojin Lee: Yes. “No benchmark-specific.”


17:08 Wei Chen: Also, we should avoid implying competitor doesn’t optimize. Like, no shade.

17:12 Soojin Lee: Yep.


17:15 (brief tangent on naming)

17:17 Ethan Wallace: On naming, are we literally saying “latency slash dollar”? Or “latency per dollar”? I saw Slack arguing.

17:23 Soojin Lee: We’ll say “latency per dollar” in prose, and show “latency/$” as a label in charts. But we have to define it.

17:31 Nadia Rahman: Please don’t call it “value” without defining it.

17:35 Jonas Weber: And don’t call it “efficiency score.” That’s vague.

17:38 Ethan Wallace: Fine.


17:42 Soojin Lee: Okay I think we have enough to lock v1. Let’s do a quick recap with decisions.

17:48 Soojin Lee: Decisions I heard:
1) Workload buckets: 1k/256, 4k/512, 8k/1k with prefill-heavy, decode-heavy, balanced mixes.
2) Concurrency: headline uses 8. Additional views at 1 and 32.
3) Prompt set: v3 “production mix” with documented sampling rules + exclusions; publish manifest/hashes not raw prompts.
4) Warmup excluded; measure steady-state.
5) Variance: 5 repeats; report median; publish p50 + p95; include range/tooltips; stability gate rerun if p95 variance > ~7% (confirm).
6) Streaming metrics: include as optional toggle/appendix, not headline.
7) Disclaimers: results vary by workload/region/concurrency; not an SLA; list price assumptions for any cost normalization; no benchmark-specific tuning; clarify cross-request prefix cache vs KV cache.

18:36 Claire Dubois: That matches my notes.

18:38 Rina Kobayashi: Yep.

18:39 Nadia Rahman: Yes, with the note I’ll confirm the exact numerator choice for latency/$—p50 vs p95—and align with Jonas.

18:46 Jonas Weber: We can do p50 in the score but always show p95 adjacent. We’ll decide after we see noise.

18:53 Ethan Wallace: Please tell me soon.

18:55 Soojin Lee: We will.


19:00 Soojin Lee: Action items—Claire posts the workload grid, Rina locks prompt set manifest, Nadia writes the one-paragraph metric explainer, Elliot and Wei draft disclaimers language. I’ll set up legal pre-read once we have text.

19:14 Talia Benson: I’ll also message Vanessa that we’re leaning into five repeats so capacity reservations need to assume that.

19:19 Soojin Lee: Great. Thanks all.

19:22 Ethan Wallace: Thank you.

19:23 Jonas Weber: Thanks.

19:24 (meeting ends; some off-mic chatter)
